title: Good to Great
author: Jim Collins
theme: Ordinary companies become great not through dramatic moves or charismatic leaders but through disciplined people, disciplined thought and disciplined action sustained over many years.
summary: Jim Collins and his research team set out to answer a hard question: can a merely good company become a great one, and if so, how? They searched decades of stock market data for firms that had performed at an average level for years and then, after a clear turning point, beat the market by a wide margin for at least fifteen years. Only eleven companies qualified. Each was compared with a similar firm in the same industry that had the same chance but failed to make the leap.

The first finding concerned leadership. The great companies were led by what Collins calls Level 5 leaders, who combine personal modesty with an intense determination to see the company succeed. They credit others for success and take the blame for failure themselves.
Second, these leaders decided who would be on the team before deciding where to take the company. Getting the right people in the right seats, and the wrong people out, came before strategy.
Third, the great companies faced reality squarely. They kept an unshakeable belief that they would win in the end while honestly confronting the harshest facts of their present situation.

Fourth, each found a simple, clear concept at the overlap of three circles: what it could be the best in the world at, what drove its economic engine, and what its people cared deeply about. Collins calls this the hedgehog concept.
Fifth, they built a culture of discipline, giving disciplined people freedom within a clear framework rather than relying on heavy rules. Technology was used to speed up momentum, never to create it.

Finally, the transformation never came from one big event. It resembled pushing a heavy flywheel, where steady effort in a consistent direction slowly builds unstoppable momentum. The comparison firms, by contrast, lurched between new programmes and saviours.
Collins concludes that greatness is largely a matter of conscious choice and discipline.
takeaway: Put the right people first, face hard facts, focus on what you can be best at, and push the flywheel patiently in one direction.

questions.q: How did Collins's team identify the companies studied in the book?
options: By surveying chief executives about their reputations
By picking the largest firms in each industry
By finding firms whose long period of average results was followed by sustained market-beating returns
By selecting companies founded by famous entrepreneurs
questions.why: The study used stock performance data to find firms that shifted from average results to at least fifteen years of exceptional returns.

questions.q: What combination of qualities defines a Level 5 leader?
options: Personal humility and fierce professional will
Charisma and a strong public profile
Technical brilliance and risk-taking
Strict control and detailed rules
questions.why: Collins found that the leaders of great companies were modest about themselves but relentlessly determined about the company's success.

questions.q: What does the principle 'first who, then what' recommend?
options: Set the strategy first, then hire people to execute it
Let customers decide the company's direction
Copy the hiring practices of competitors
Get the right people on board before deciding where to go
questions.why: Great companies built the right team first, believing that the right people would help find and adapt the right direction.

questions.q: Why did the research include comparison companies?
options: To show which industries were growing fastest
To isolate what distinguished the great firms from similar firms with the same opportunities
To estimate the total size of each market
To rank companies by number of employees
questions.why: Contrasting each great company with a similar firm that did not make the leap revealed the factors that actually made the difference.

questions.q: The idea of confronting the brutal facts while keeping faith in eventual success is linked in the book to:
options: The flywheel
The hedgehog concept
The Stockdale Paradox
The doom loop
questions.why: Collins uses the Stockdale Paradox to describe holding unwavering belief in the end goal alongside honest acceptance of current reality.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three circles of the hedgehog concept?
options: What you are deeply passionate about
What your competitors are currently doing
What you can be the best in the world at
What drives your economic engine
questions.why: The hedgehog concept sits at the overlap of passion, being best in the world, and the economic engine; competitors' actions are not one of the circles.

questions.q: How does a culture of discipline work in great companies, according to Collins?
options: Managers tightly supervise every task
Employees follow detailed rulebooks
Discipline is imposed only during crises
Self-disciplined people are given freedom within a clear framework
questions.why: Collins argues that with disciplined people, heavy bureaucracy becomes unnecessary; they act responsibly within agreed boundaries.

questions.q: What role did technology play in the good-to-great transformations?
options: It accelerated momentum but was not the cause of it
It was the main trigger of every transformation
It was largely ignored by the great companies
It replaced the need for good people
questions.why: The great companies used carefully chosen technologies to speed up progress that already rested on their core concept.

questions.q: What does the flywheel image describe?
options: A sudden breakthrough after one bold decision
Momentum built up gradually by consistent effort in one direction
Frequent changes in strategy to stay ahead
A cycle of hiring and firing leaders
questions.why: Collins found no single defining moment; progress came from steady, cumulative pushes that eventually produced breakthrough momentum.

questions.q: What pattern did Collins observe in the comparison companies?
options: They stuck to a single concept for decades
They avoided acquisitions completely
They lurched between new programmes, leaders and big moves
They hired only Level 5 leaders
questions.why: The comparison firms fell into a doom loop of reactive changes and searches for a saviour instead of building consistent momentum.
